   4. `channel-unknown`: the channel is neither in the persona's heard set (`heardChannels(key)`, see Inbound step 4) nor among its stored choices (`storedChannels(key)`): `…: channel "<C…>" is not known: it is not a channel this persona has heard a message from in fungible mode, or holds a choice for. Only a public or private channel that is not externally shared can be set.` (`channelDeliveryChannelRefusal`). The channel is echoed only when it matches `ECHOABLE_CHANNEL_RE` (`^[A-Z0-9]{1,24}$`); otherwise it reads `the channel is not known (the value given is not shown)`.
4. **Storing the choice** (b.deo SRI-504): one `store.set(key, channel, delivery, channelDeliveryDeclarationOf(persona))`, the persona's declaration from the configuration in effect. A value already stored is written like any other.
   - A failed write (b.deo SRI-506) is the tool error `Tool "set_channel_delivery" failed for persona "<name>" (key=<key>): the stored-choice file "<path>" could not be written, so the choice was not stored and channel delivery is unchanged.` (`channelDeliveryWriteFailedText`); the store logs its own `[slack] channel-delivery:` failed-write line, and memory is unchanged.
   - A store that answers unreadable gives the `store-unreadable` refusal, and one that refuses an input (`invalid`) gives `…: the choice was not stored (the store refused its <field>), so channel delivery is unchanged.` (`channelDeliveryNotStoredText`).
5. **The result and the loop guard.** After a stored write the persona's channel delivery there is `channelDeliveryFor(key, channel, { fungibleDestinations: fungibleDestinationsOf(<fungible mode>, <applied personas>), storedChoices: store })`, the one rule the routing uses (`delivery-decision.ts`), over the applied personas of the configuration in effect (`getAppliedPersonas`). The result text is `Stored <stored> as your channel delivery for channel <channel>. From the next message in that channel, your channel delivery there is <delivery>.` (`channelDeliverySetResultText`); when the loop guard holds the channel, it ends `…there is mentions: the channel is another persona's fungible destination, where its permission prompts and notices go, so the loop guard holds it at mentions whatever is stored.`
6. **The line** (b.deo SRI-505, SRI-902): after the write, one `persona-channel-delivery-set` line through `SessionToolDeps.log` (production `console.error`, the server log's `[slack]` stream; nothing is posted to Slack), built by `formatPersonaDiagnostic` with `channelDeliverySetCause`: `[slack] persona-channel-delivery-set: personas[<i>] "<name>" (key=<key>): stored choice for channel <id> set from <none|mentions|all> to <mentions|all>, at channel delivery <mentions|all> after the loop guard`. `none` (`NO_STORED_CHOICE`) is a channel with no stored choice before the call. This line is the tool's; the store's own lines are under Logging, [Stored-choice file lines](#stored-choice-file-lines-bdeo-sri-904-sri-905).
7. **Dry run** (b.deo SRI-507) is not consulted: the choice is stored and logged as outside it, and no Slack call is made either way.

The choice applies from the next event in that channel (Inbound step 4). It lives only in `channel-delivery.json`, never in `config.json`; when it is dropped is under Configuration, [channel-delivery.json](#channel-deliveryjson-state_dirchannel-deliveryjson).

### Slack Reply Guard (Stop hook)

`stop-hooks/slack-reply-guard.sh` runs in every bot session whose config dir the bootstrap patched: the start pass (startup step 4a-ter) or the launch-time pass before each spawn or resume. It reads stdin once, reads the transcript once with a single `jq` pass, and fails open (exit 0) on any error, missing input, or malformed transcript. Its only exit-2 path is step 8.

1. **Per-persona gate.** The first argument is the record directory `<state dir>/reply-guard`. The guard continues only when the argument is non-empty, `CSCB_PERSONA` matches `^[a-z0-9_]{1,49}$`, and the record `<dir>/<CSCB_PERSONA>` is a regular, readable file reading exactly `true` (one trailing newline tolerated). Every other case, `false` included, exits 0 silently. How the record is written and deleted: see Configuration, reply-guard/<key>; a persona teardown deletes it.
2. **jq check.** A missing `jq` logs one stderr line and exits 0. A persona stopped at step 1 never gets this warning.
3. **Retry pass-through.** `stop_hook_active=true` exits 0 immediately, so the reminder fires at most once per turn. A missing, unreadable or empty transcript also exits 0.
4. **Trigger run.** A real user entry has `type=="user"`, is not `isSidechain` or `isCompactSummary`, and has at least one text block. The run is every real user entry after the nearest non-sidechain assistant entry preceding the latest real user entry. Claude Code can write queued channel messages as consecutive user entries, so the run can hold several. Tool-result-only entries, sidechain entries, and compaction summaries neither join nor end the run.
5. **Envelope.** Only an opening `<channel …>` tag at the very start of an entry's text (after optional whitespace) is an envelope; a tag later in the text is quoted body and is ignored. The tag is read as whitespace-led `name="value"` pairs, left to right. Names are compared whole (`via` never matches inside a longer name), the first of a repeated name wins, and text inside one attribute's value is never read as another attribute. The envelope is Slack iff its `source` starts with `slack`.
6. **`via` test.** A Slack envelope that carries `via` is a delivered Slack message, even when the value is empty or unknown. One without `via` is injected (a scheduled prompt or an `/interject` message), whatever its `user` or `ts`. No delivered Slack message in the run → exit 0.
7. **Reply check.** An assistant `tool_use` named `mcp__slack-channel-router__reply` anywhere after the earliest delivered Slack entry in the run → exit 0. Because the whole run is checked, an injected message queued right after a delivered one does not hide it.
8. **Reminder.** Otherwise exit 2 with a declinable reminder on stderr. The `via` of the last delivered Slack envelope in the run picks the wording: one each for `dm`, `mention`, `broadcast`, `receive_all_shared` and `receive_all`, and the generic channel wording for any other value. When that envelope's `chat_id` matches `^[A-Z0-9]+$`, the wording adds `(conversation <chat_id>)` for `dm` or `(channel <chat_id>)` otherwise; a missing or non-matching `chat_id` is left out. The raw `via` value is never echoed. README.md's Slack Reply Guard section shows the texts.

The envelope is rendered by the Claude Code harness from the MCP notification's `meta`. The tag name `channel` and the attribute names the guard reads (`source`, `via`, `chat_id`) are a harness-owned contract. The guard depends on CSCB never putting `via` on injected meta: `/interject`, and cron through it, sends only `user` and `ts` (see [POST /interject](#post-interject)). It also relies on the harness escaping attribute values, since a value is read up to the next `"`.

A confirmed change to a persona's `stop_hook_bootstrap` or `claude_config_dir` (own or inherited) reaches the guard at the persona's next launch, which writes its record and runs the install rule; the apply itself writes nothing (see [Next-launch and server-wide settings](#next-launch-and-server-wide-settings-bav2-sr-86-as-amended-by-bdeo-sri-201-sri-203)).

Accepted limit: launched-with directories are kept in memory only and are not persisted. After a confirmed `claude_config_dir` change and a plain server restart, a still-running instance no longer counts toward the old directory it launched with. When every persona still counted toward that directory is disabled, the next pass that evaluates it (the restart's start pass, or a launch pass for a neighbour whose effective or launched-with directory it is) removes the managed Stop hook from under the instance; only that instance's reply reminder is lost, until its next launch. The README (Slack Reply Guard, Timing) and the debugging skill document it for operators.

### Permission Relay (SR-2)

Driven by polling against the agent-director Client + Block Kit click → `decide()`. The previous HTTP long-poll + hook script architecture has been deleted. Per-row Slack prompts: N concurrent `tool_use` blocks in one Claude Code assistant response produce N Slack messages, each independently allow/deny-able.

#### Wire surface (paired AD release)

CSCB consumes four AD verbs:

- `client.list({ state: ['check_permission'], label: ['service=cscb'] })` — returns spawn rows in the permission state.
- `client.get({ claude_instance_id })` — returns the row plus a plural `permission_requests` projection. Each element carries `request_token`, `request_id`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `requested_at`. The array may be empty (spawn has no open prompts). `null` / `undefined` in the slot is non-conforming.
- `client.decide({ claude_instance_id, decision, request_token })` — JSON snake `request_token`, CLI `--request-token`. Always required; absence yields `ErrInvalidFlags`. The wrapper `decideWithToken` in `agent-director-client.ts` is the single decide-wire serializer (SR-7.2).
- `client.getPermission({ request_token })` — single-row read, no state filter. Returns full PermissionRequestInfo plus `decision`, `decision_reason`, and `decided_at`. Not-found surfaces as `ErrPermissionRequestNotFound` (matched via `isErrPermissionRequestNotFound`).

#### In-memory state (SR-1)

`livePermissions: Map<string, LivePermission>` keyed on a composite `(claude_instance_id, request_token)` encoded by `makeCompositeKey` (null-byte separator — neither component can contain `\x00`). One entry per outstanding Slack prompt. `LivePermission` carries `claudeInstanceId`, `requestToken`, `personaKey` (the persona whose client posted the prompt; closing updates go through it), `channelId` (the conversation the prompt was posted in: the channel, or the `D…` DM conversation), `messageTs`, `requestId` (log-only — never used for routing, keying, action-id encoding, or decide-wire payload per SR-1.4), and a `handled` flag. Lifecycle helpers `getLivePermission(cid, token)`, `markHandled(cid, token)`, and `dropPermission(cid, token)` all operate on the composite key. The tick is the sole owner of `dropPermission`; the click handler may only call `markHandled` (SR-1.2).

The recorded `personaKey` and `channelId` are the only routing a posted prompt keeps. The closing update (step 5) and the click updates ([Click handler](#click-handler-sr-4)) go to that conversation through that persona's client and never resolve the persona's destination again or read its DMs switch. So a prompt stays where it was posted and stays answerable after the persona's destination changes, a confirmed switch change of the channel mode included (b.deo SRI-703), and a prompt posted in a DM is still updated after `dm.enabled` is turned off (b.av2 SR-5.1 exception, as amended by b.deo SRI-601: an update is not a post). The DMs-off scope that does not apply here is the MCP tools' outbound scoping (`checkPersonaTarget`, b.av2 SR-5.1 as amended by b.deo SRI-601; see Outbound), which govern posts, reads and DM opens made by a session, not updates to prompts the server already posted.

**Teardown.** A persona teardown drops the persona's tracked prompts, their not-posted, payload-rejection and failure records and its wedge state (`forgetPersonaPrompts`) with no closing update, so their Slack messages stay as posted. A later click on one has no effect: a click arrives only on the Slack connection of the persona that posted the prompt (b.av2 SR-7.1 as amended by b.deo SRI-701 to SRI-703), and the teardown closed it.

#### Per-tick flow (SR-2)

1. `list()` → spawns currently in `check_permission`.
2. For each spawn, resolve the persona from the row's `persona` label through the applied persona set (`PollerDeps.getPersona`, read every tick; b.av2 SR-7.1 as amended by b.deo SRI-701 to SRI-703). The `channel` label is never read. A row with no `persona` label logs `[slack] permission-poller: spawn <id> has no persona label — skipping`, and one naming no applied persona logs `[slack] permission-poller: spawn <id> names no applied persona (persona=<key>) — skipping`; either is skipped this tick with no `get`. The no-label line is logged once per instance ID while the row stays listed (`noLabelLogged`, b.1ix), since the start sweep keeps a pre-persona row and one can sit in `check_permission` indefinitely; an ID that a successful `list()` no longer holds is forgotten, so the row logs again if it comes back, and a failed `list()` forgets nothing. A spawn naming a persona that is no longer applied is treated like a non-conforming spawn (step 3): its live entries are exempt from the closing sweep and its wedge state is kept, since its requests may still be open in agent-director, until the persona's teardown (apply step 2) drops them. A spawn with no `persona` label gets no such exemption. A spawn whose persona is applied but not up (`PollerDeps.isPersonaUp`, the server's shared up predicate; b.av2 SR-6.4) is skipped with no `get`: nothing is posted under any identity, its instance keeps running, and its wedge detector gets no tick. Its live entries are exempt from the closing sweep and its wedge state is kept, whether or not its spawn is listed this tick, because its requests are still open in agent-director. On the first tick after the persona is up its rows are read again: a prompt opened while it was down posts then, and a tracked prompt that closed meanwhile gets its verdict through step 5. The skip emits no trail event and no `cscb.poller.row_decision`. It logs once when it starts, `[slack] permission-poller: persona "<name>" (key=<key>) is not up — skipping its rows and holding its tracked prompts until it is up`, and once when it ends, `[slack] permission-poller: persona "<name>" (key=<key>) is up again — polling its rows again` (or `[slack] permission-poller: persona=<key> is no longer applied — no longer skipping its rows` when the persona left the applied set). Then `get()` returns the plural `permission_requests` projection, inside `withOutageDetection` keyed by the persona key. The poller's calls (`get`, `get-permission`) are not tmux-touching, so their success clears `ad-unreachable` but never `tmux-unavailable`.
3. Non-conforming response (`permission_requests` is `null` or `undefined`): log + skip processing for that spawn this tick. The spawn's existing live entries are excluded from the closure sweep below (no state mutation — SR-2.1). A spawn naming a persona that is no longer applied (step 2) gets the same exemption.
4. For each row in `permission_requests`, compute the composite key. If not in `livePermissions`, route it to the persona's destination through the shared destination resolver (`src/persona-destination.ts`, the same resolver and DM cache the notifier uses):
   - **Re-resolve after awaits (AC 58):** a confirmed reload's step 1 can swap the applied set during any await of the tick. The poller re-reads the persona (`getPersona(key)`) after the agent-director `get`, before the wedge attempt of an empty projection and before each prompt post, so each goes to the destination applied now. A persona gone by then is handled as a row naming no applied persona (step 2): the same line, its live entries exempt from the closing sweep and its wedge state kept, and its remaining prompts in that row are not posted. The not-up check uses the read at the start of the row.
   - **Destination:** the one destination rule (`personaDestinationOf`, b.av2 SR-7.1 as amended by b.deo SRI-701, SRI-702) over the configuration in effect at the attempt names it: the persona's `permission_prompts` in declarative mode, its `invited.permission_prompts` (`"dm"` when absent) in fungible mode. A channel there is that channel; in fungible mode it needs no listing in any section, only the app's membership. `dm` is the persona's DM conversation with `dm.contact`, obtained with `conversations.open` on the persona's client. Slack returns the existing conversation, or opens one when none exists, so a DM-only persona's first prompt is delivered with no earlier DM. The resolved conversation is cached per persona and contact: later prompts reuse it with no second open, concurrent posts share one in-flight open, and a changed contact opens afresh (see the Module Map entry for what drops the cache).
   - **Post:** ask the destination hold for an attempt (`begin(key)`); while the persona is held, stop here (see **Held persona** below). Otherwise emit the `post_attempted` row decision, then post one `chat.postMessage` per row (no coalescing — SR-2.2) through the persona's own client (`PollerDeps.clientFor(key)`, the connection manager's long-lived client for that persona) to the destination conversation — the channel, or the returned `D…` ID, never the contact's user ID — and insert one map entry recording that conversation. For a `dm` destination the `conversations.open`, when one is needed, comes before the post on the same client. A failed open or post emits one `ok:false` `cscb.chat_post.attempted` and inserts no map entry, so the row is still untracked on the next tick; the attempt reports its outcome to the hold. A destination failure (every failed open, and every failed post except a payload error) is logged only by the hold, as its one `persona-destination-failed` line per episode, and holds the persona. A post that fails for the message itself (`MESSAGE_PAYLOAD_ERRORS`, such as `invalid_blocks` or `msg_too_long`) holds nothing, and that message is never posted again (see **Payload error** below).
   - **Prompt text (b.zmq):** the section is a header naming the tool, `🤖🛠️ *<tool>*`, over a summary of its input in backticks: Bash's `command`, Edit's or Write's `file_path`, otherwise (or when that field is absent) the input's JSON, at most `PROMPT_JSON_SUMMARY_MAX` (500) characters of it. A summary that would take the section past Slack's section-text limit, `SLACK_SECTION_TEXT_MAX` (3000; the header, backticks and marker counted), or a JSON summary over 500, is cut, never splitting a surrogate pair, and followed by ` … (truncated, <shown> of <total> chars shown)`. A tool name over `PROMPT_TOOL_NAME_MAX` (200) is cut to end `…`, in the header and in the message's `text`, `🤖🛠️ permission request: <tool>`. The builder is `buildPermissionBlocks`.
   - **Payload error (b.zmq):** the rejection is recorded for the request (`payloadRejections`) before its line is logged, so the rejected message is never posted again. The full prompt's rejection logs `[slack] permission-poller: chat.postMessage failed for <id> token=<token> (the prompt's message was rejected; a short prompt naming the tool is posted instead)<tail>` (`buildPromptRejectedLine`), and the request's next attempt (the next tick, through the hold as usual) posts the short prompt (`buildFallbackPermissionBlocks`): the same header over `_The tool input is not shown: Slack rejected the full prompt (<code>)._`, with the same Allow and Deny buttons, tracked and closed like any prompt. When Slack rejects the short prompt's message too, the poller logs `[slack] permission-poller: chat.postMessage failed for <id> token=<token> (the short prompt's message was rejected too; nothing more is posted for this request)<tail>` (`buildFallbackPromptRejectedLine`) and attempts nothing more for the request (no `post_attempted`, no trail event, no line) while it is observed. Each attempt that reaches Slack still emits its one `cscb.chat_post.attempted`. `<tail>` is `describeDestinationFailure`'s ` (reason=<reason>): <description>`. The record is forgotten once the request posts, or once it is no longer observed (a spawn skipped this tick keeps it), so a request listed again tries its full prompt.
   - **Held persona** (an episode is open and its retry is not due yet, or a retry for it is already in flight; see [Destination hold](#destination-hold-bav2-sr-71-failures-as-amended-by-bdeo-sri-702-sri-703)): no Slack call, no `post_attempted`, no trail event, no line and no map entry. The prompt stays untracked and is derived again on each tick; the first tick at or after the retry's due time makes the retry, one prompt at a time per persona. The poller sets no timer of its own for this: retries of prompts ride on the tick. A request that stops being pending while its persona is held (decided in the terminal, timed out, or its spawn gone) is simply no longer derived, so it is never posted. This check comes after the refused-destination and client checks below.
   - **Refused `dm` destination** (`dm.enabled` not true or no `dm.contact`; the loader rejects both, in fungible mode a defaulted `"dm"` included, so this is a defensive guard, checked first with the resolver's `refusalOf`, `dmDestinationRefusal` over the configuration in effect): no Slack call, no `post_attempted`, no map entry. Logged once per open request, naming the setting in force (`destinationSettingFrom`; b.deo SRI-906): `[slack] permission-poller: "<name>" (key=<key>) has <permission_prompts|invited.permission_prompts> set to "dm" but <dm.enabled is not true|dm.contact is not set> — prompt for <id> (request_token=<token>) not posted and no DM opened`.
   - **Client unavailable** (`clientFor` returns undefined; a persona that is not up is already skipped in step 2, so this is a guard for a persona whose connection stops serving between the two checks): no Slack call, no `post_attempted`, no map entry, so a later tick retries. Logged once per open request: `[slack] permission-poller: no Slack client for "<name>" (key=<key>) — prompt for <id> (request_token=<token>) not posted; retrying on a later tick`.

   The once-per-request record of an unposted prompt is forgotten when the prompt posts or the request is no longer observed (a spawn skipped this tick keeps its records); a changed reason logs again. If the composite key is already in `livePermissions`: no-op (duplicate-tick safe). An empty projection produces no posting activity but does not exclude the spawn's live entries from closure reconciliation. An empty projection also feeds the wedge detector (below).
5. **Set-diff closure reconciliation (SR-2.4):** `tokens_in_livePermissions − tokens_seen_this_tick = newly_closed_tokens` (with non-conforming spawns' entries protected per step 3, and a not-up persona's entries held per step 2). For each newly-closed token, call `getPermission(request_token)` inside `withOutageDetection` keyed by `entry.personaKey`. On success, render the verdict (below) via one `chat.update` against `entry.channelId` + `entry.messageTs` through the client of the persona that posted it (`clientFor(entry.personaKey)`), then drop the entry. When that client is unavailable, no update is made, `[slack] permission-poller: no Slack client for "<name>" (key=<key>) — closure update for <id> token=<token> (verdict=<tag>) skipped` is logged (`persona=<key>` in place of the name and key when the persona is no longer applied), and the entry is still dropped (agent-director has already closed the request). On `ErrPermissionRequestNotFound`: render generic deny, drop, do not retry. On transient error: leave the entry alive — the next tick retries.

**One failure stays with its row or request (b.zmq).** A throw while handling one open request (its prompt built, posted or trailed), one row outside its requests (its persona, its `get` result, its stuck-prompt warning) or one closed entry in step 5 is caught there, and the tick goes on with the other rows and requests, the wedge re-arm and step 5. A hold attempt the throw interrupted is still released. Each line ends in the thrown value's `describeThrownValue`, and a logger that throws on it falls back to `console.error`:

- Request (`buildPromptFailedLine`): `[slack] permission-poller: prompt for <id> (request_token=<token>) failed — the tick goes on; a later tick tries it again unless it was posted: <description>`, once per request (`failedRequests`). A post clears the record; a throw after the post (its success trail event) records it again, and the prompt, tracked before that event, is not posted again. The record stays while the request is observed or tracked and goes once it is neither, or at the persona's teardown. The request counts as observed, so its tracked prompt is not swept.
- Row (`buildSpawnFailedLine`): `[slack] permission-poller: spawn <id> failed — the tick goes on, its tracked prompts and stuck-prompt state kept as if not read this tick: <description>`, once while the row keeps failing; again after a tick it doesn't (`failedRows`). The row counts as not read this tick (step 3): its live entries are exempt from step 5 and its wedge state is kept.
- Closed entry (`buildClosingFailedLine`): `[slack] permission-poller: closing prompt for <id> token=<token> failed — kept for the next tick, the tick goes on: <description>`, once per entry, through its own record (`failedClosings`), kept apart from `failedRequests` so a prompt failure recorded for the same request cannot silence it. The record goes when the entry is dropped (`dropPermission`), at the persona's teardown (`forgetPersonaPrompts`) or at `_resetPollerState`. The entry stays alive and step 5 tries it again next tick.

A throw past these catches (the listing not iterable, a throw in the wedge re-arm) ends that tick only. The interval runs `runTick(deps).catch(…)` (`noteTickFailure`), which logs `[slack] permission-poller: tick failed — the rest of it skipped: <description>` (`buildTickFailedLine`) once until a tick runs to its end, so no tick leaves an unhandled rejection.

The six b.zmq lines (these four and step 4's two payload-rejection lines) come only from their exported, pure builders in `src/permission-poller.ts`; `tests/permission-poller.test.ts` pins each builder's output against the text the debugging skill quotes (b.jg5 SRJ-1014).

#### Verdict rendering (SR-5)

The closure `chat.update` produces four visually-distinct surfaces driven by `decision` + `decision_reason`:

| `decision` | `decision_reason` | Rendering |
|---|---|---|
| `allow` | `null` | `*Permission* — Allowed` |
| `deny` | `'operator'` | `*Permission* — Denied by operator` |
| `deny` | `'timeout'` | `⏱ *Permission* — Timed out` |
| `deny` | `'find_missing'` | `🪦 *Permission* — Session ended` |
| anything else | anything else | `*Permission* — Denied (closed)` (fail-closed, log) |

`ErrPermissionRequestNotFound` collapses to the same generic-deny rendering (fail-closed log + drop, no retry). `decision_reason` is read verbatim from AD; CSCB does not derive, override, or infer it (SR-5.1). Unknown enum values do not crash the poller (SR-5.2). The `chat.update` targets only the closed row's `messageTs`; sibling rows are never touched in response to one row's closure (SR-5.3).

#### Click handler (SR-4)

`handlePermissionClick` decodes `(decision, claude_instance_id, request_token)` from the action_id and calls `decideWithToken(client, { claude_instance_id, decision, request_token })` unconditionally — this is the click's only AD interaction (SR-4.3). No `get` refetch, no "already decided" branch.

The click resolves through the receiving persona (b.av2 SR-7.1 as amended by b.deo SRI-701 to SRI-703): `ClickDeps.receivingPersonaKey` looked up with `getPersona`. The click arrives on the owning persona's connection through its `interactive` event, and the event router (`src/persona-event-router.ts`) passes that connection's persona key, so a click that reaches another persona's connection is refused below. Parsing comes first: an action_id that does not parse returns `false` before any persona is resolved. After the `cscb.click_handler.invoked` event:

- A receiving persona that cannot be resolved is logged and the click is bypassed (no decide, no update): `[slack] permission-click-handler: cannot resolve the receiving persona (receiving key=<key>, claude_instance_id=<id>, action_id=<action_id>, request_token=<token>) — logging and bypassing this click. This is a CSCB bug — investigate.`
- A click whose instance ID is not the receiving persona's `cscb_<key>` fails closed — neither decided nor updated, so the request stays open until agent-director times it out: `[slack] permission-click-handler: click for <id> received for "<name>" (key=<key>) (instance cscb_<key>) — not deciding (request_token=<token>)`.
- Otherwise `decideWithToken` runs inside `withOutageDetection` keyed by the persona key, declared as `decide`, so click-path outage state is per persona (a successful `decide` clears `ad-unreachable` but never `tmux-unavailable`, since `decide` is not tmux-touching), and every `chat.update` below (verdict and relay-fallen-back repaint) goes through that persona's client (`ClickDeps.clientFor`) to the conversation and `ts` recorded on the live entry. A prompt posted in a DM is handled the same way, with no post and no `conversations.open` (see [In-memory state](#in-memory-state-sr-1)). When the client is unavailable, no update is made and `markHandled` is not called; one line is logged, `[slack] permission-click: no Slack client for "<name>" (key=<key>) — update for <id> (request_token=<token>, verdict=<tag>) skipped; the next poller tick reconciles the rendering`.

Decide outcomes:

- `ErrAlreadyDecided` → swallowed silently. The next tick's reconciliation (SR-2.4) owns the visible Slack state.
- `ErrRelayFallenBack` (b.qi1) → logged loudly, prompt message repainted, no session-level action. See the note below.
- `ErrInvalidFlags` → logged once, no retry, no operator-visible signal. The order is: the trail event (emitted before the branch), the log line, then the `ErrInvalidFlags` step (`classifyWithInvalidFlagsRecheck`, `src/ad-error-class.ts`, b.jg5 SRJ-204 / SRJ-104) is started and not awaited: one immediate agent-director version re-check, then class UNCLASSIFIED. It is not awaited because the event router (`routeInteractive`, `src/persona-event-router.ts`) acks the Slack interactive payload only after the handler returns, and a slow re-check would hold that ack past Slack's window; the step never rejects, and a `.catch` guards against an unhandled rejection. A re-check that stops (a binary below the Phase 1 floor or too old) stops the server as the runtime re-check defines; any other answer changes nothing here. The handler returns true, makes no retry and no `chat.update`. See [Agent-director error classes](#agent-director-error-classes-bjg5-srj-104).
- `ErrAmbiguousRequest` → logged once, no retry, no operator-visible signal.
- Unknown error types → logged, no retry.

On a successful decide *and* a live entry present, the handler renders one `chat.update` against just that row's `messageTs` (SR-4.5) carrying text byte-identical to the poller's SR-2.4 verdict surface — `*Permission* — Allowed` for allow, `*Permission* — Denied by operator` for deny — then calls `markHandled`. Matching the verdict text exactly means there is no visible flicker when the next tick's reconciliation lands on the same message. A stale click (no entry in `livePermissions`) still fires the decide call with the decoded token — AD is the source of truth and returns idempotent results — but produces no `chat.update` from the click path; the next tick's verdict rendering handles the message.

**b.qi1 `ErrRelayFallenBack` — loud surfacing, no session-level action.** agent-director 0.10.0 raises this from `decide` when the request's relay window has elapsed: Claude Code already gave up on the relay and re-asked at its own tmux pane, so AD refuses to record a verdict nothing will read. It is a *decide-path* error, not a spawn error — the spawn ladder in [Server-Managed Startup](#server-managed-startup-sr-11-event-1) cannot see it, and `handlePermissionClick` is its only reachable call site. The spawn itself is alive and healthy; only that one prompt can no longer be answered from Slack. The handler therefore logs a `[slack]`-prefixed line, emits `cscb.ad_decide.attempted{result_class:"ErrRelayFallenBack"}`, and — when a live entry is still present — renders one `chat.update` over that row's `messageTs` reading `*Permission* — relay window elapsed; answer this prompt at the session's tmux pane`, stripping the now-inert buttons, tagged `click_handler_relay_fallen_back`.

No delete, no respawn, no retry. Re-deciding fails identically (the window is already closed), and the handler kills and launches nothing, so a healthy session is never ended over one un-relayed prompt. `markHandled` is deliberately **not** called: this is not a verdict and the AD request row stays open, so a later poller closure (timeout, `find_missing`, or the answer given at the pane) must remain free to render over the same message.

The Slack user id is intentionally NOT surfaced in the rendered text. An earlier draft of this design rendered "Allowed by <user>" / "Denied by <user>" as immediate operator feedback, but the SR-2.4 reconciler overwrites the message one tick later with the user-less verdict surface, producing visible flicker for the operator who clicked. The simpler, flicker-free design renders the verdict text on both the click path and the reconciliation path.

#### Wedge detector (b.fae F4)

A spawn can wedge permanently in `check_permission` with an **empty** `permission_requests` array: the underlying cause is a permission decision that AD recorded but could not deliver (the relay hook was killed before AD's poll deadline), leaving Claude Code blocked on a native TUI prompt with no open AD row and no hook that will ever fire again to advance state. To the poller's row handling this is a valid conforming response with zero rows, which posts, logs and records nothing, so the bot would look dead with no signal; the wedge detector below is what reports it.

The detector counts consecutive ticks a spawn is observed in `check_permission` with an empty projection. The trip threshold is derived from the poll interval — `wedgeTripTicks(intervalMs) = max(5, ceil(90000 / intervalMs))`, roughly 90 s of wall-clock — because a genuine wedge takes minutes to develop while a normal decided-then-closing spawn passes through the empty state only briefly. The counter is reset **only on a positive observation** that the spawn is not wedged — open rows present, its state changed, or it's confirmed gone via `ErrSpawnNotFound`. A spawn skipped in a tick because of a transient `get` error or a non-conforming response does **not** have its counter reset, so a single flaky AD connection can't silently defer a genuine wedge alarm. A spawn whose persona is not up (b.av2 SR-6.4) is neither counted nor reset: its state is held, listed or not, until the persona is up.

On trip it logs `[slack] permission-poller: spawn <id> for "<name>" (key=<key>) wedged in check_permission with zero open rows for <n> ticks (~<s>s) — sending one-shot warning` and sends a **one-shot** warning to the persona's destination (b.av2 SR-7.2). The warning text names the persona: `Persona "<name>" (key=<key>): ⚠️ This persona appears blocked on a native Claude Code permission prompt …` (`buildWedgeWarningText(persona, claudeInstanceId)`: the notifier's `formatPersonaNotice` over `buildWedgeWarningBody(claudeInstanceId)`, both exported from `src/permission-poller.ts`; the body alone is what the teardown window gets). It is one top-level message posted through the persona's client and the shared destination resolver to the persona's destination, by the one destination rule in the mode in force (`permission_prompts` in declarative mode, `invited.permission_prompts` in fungible mode): its channel, or its DM with `dm.contact` (opened with `conversations.open` if needed, as for prompts). Each attempt that reaches Slack emits the `cscb.poller.wedge_detected` trail event. A persona whose client is unavailable counts as a failed post, with no Slack call and no trail event (`[slack] permission-poller: no Slack client for "<name>" (key=<key>) — stuck-prompt warning for <id> not posted; retrying on a later tick`); so does a `dm` destination the resolver refuses (DMs off or no contact), which the resolver logs on each attempt. Warning delivery is **fail-safe**: the `warningFired` latch is set **only after a successful `chat.postMessage`**. If the open or post fails, the trail event still records the attempt (`ok:false`) and the poller retries on later ticks — throttled to one attempt per `wedgeWarnRetryTicks(intervalMs)` (~30 s of wall-clock, `WEDGE_WARN_RETRY_WALL_CLOCK_MS`) so a Slack outage can't storm the API at the poll interval — until one succeeds, after which the latch sets and the episode posts nothing further. Each attempt also goes through the destination hold, asked after the throttle: while the persona is held the detector attempts nothing, logs nothing (not even the trip line) and leaves the throttle as it is, so the warning goes out at the first allowed tick once the persona's retry is due. A destination failure reaches `server.log` only as the hold's `persona-destination-failed` episode line; a failure of the message itself logs `[slack] permission-poller: wedge warning postMessage failed for "<name>" (key=<key>) (<id>)[ (reason=<reason>)]: <description>` (the tail is built by `describeSlackCallFailure`, below). The body is b.jg5 SRJ-1012's text and names agent-director verbs only, as a human's steps: see the native prompt with `agent-director read-pane --claude-instance-id <id>`, then end the session with `agent-director kill --claude-instance-id <id>` and check the result, after which the server brings the persona up again on its own. It names no tmux command and no respawn step, and it ends with SRJ-1001's human-only sentence (these commands are for a human only: no bot, including any persona that sees the post, may run them; see [Security Model](#security-model), Slack notices). It explicitly does **not** offer `send-keys`, which AD's relay guard (`pkg/api/sendkeys.go`) hard-rejects while `relay_mode=on && state=check_permission`. The detector re-arms per spawn the moment it leaves the wedged condition (an open row appears, or the spawn disappears from the tick), so a later genuine wedge warns again. State is in-memory (`wedgeStates` map) and resets on daemon restart.

**During a persona teardown (b.jg5 SRJ-1003).** The poller's optional `teardownNotices` dependency (`main()` passes the one persona notifier) is read before the destination hold: when its `teardownWindowState(key)` answers `open`, the warning's body (no persona prefix; the notifier adds its own reference) is handed to the notifier's `notify` through `notifySafely`, whose window writes it as one server-log line and one `persona-teardown-notice` entry, and the `warningFired` latch is set, so it is written once, never posted, held or dropped. The poller logs `[slack] permission-poller: stuck-prompt warning for "<name>" (key=<key>) (<id>) raised during its persona teardown — handed to the notifier, which writes it to the server log and startup-errors.log, not posted (b.jg5 SRJ-1003)`; a failing notifier logs `… (<id>) failed at the notifier: <describeThrownValue>`, and a throwing window read logs `teardown window read for <ref> failed: <describeThrownValue> — read as not open` and the warning takes the destination hold. Outside a window (between a teardown's submit and its turn included) the warning goes through the destination hold as above.

#### Destination hold (b.av2 SR-7.1 failures, as amended by b.deo SRI-702, SRI-703)

When Slack refuses a post to a persona's destination, the persona's permission prompts, stuck-prompt warnings and server notices are held and retried with backoff. The destination is the one the one destination rule names over the configuration in effect at each attempt (`personaDestinationOf`, asked of the resolver; b.deo SRI-701, SRI-702): the persona's `permission_prompts` in declarative mode, its `invited.permission_prompts` (`"dm"` when absent) in fungible mode. After a confirmed switch change the hold tracks the setting in force, and its lines name that setting (`destination=<value>`, plus ` (invited.permission_prompts)` in fungible mode; see Logging, [Persona destination lines](#persona-destination-lines-bav2-sr-103-as-amended-by-bdeo-sri-906)). The logic is `src/persona-destination-hold.ts`; `server.ts` builds one instance and hands it to both the poller and the notifier, so a persona's prompts and notices share one episode.

**What is held.** A destination failure is any failed `conversations.open` (including an open that returns no conversation ID, `no_conversation_id`) and any failed `chat.postMessage` except a payload error about the message itself (`MESSAGE_PAYLOAD_ERRORS`: `invalid_blocks`, `msg_too_long`, `no_text` and the like). So `missing_scope` on the open (an app not re-installed with `im:write`), `not_in_channel`, `channel_not_found`, `is_archived`, other permission errors and the Slack-unreachable class are all held. In fungible mode a destination channel needs no listing, only the app's membership, so `not_in_channel` or `channel_not_found` at a fungible destination channel the app is not a member of is held like any other destination failure. A payload error neither opens nor extends an episode: a prompt's message is logged once and never posted again, its request's next attempt posting a short prompt in its place (b.zmq; Per-tick flow step 4, **Payload error**), and a notice is logged once and dropped. A refused `dm` destination (DMs off or no contact) makes no Slack call and is not a failure. The resolver does not cache a failed open, so each retry opens afresh.

**Per persona (b.av2 SR-3.3).** Each persona has its own entry: episode, retry schedule, FIFO of held notices, timer and in-flight guard. Nothing spans two personas, so one persona's episode never delays, holds or logs for another.

**Episodes and backoff.** An episode opens at a destination failure when none is open for the persona, and logs one `persona-destination-failed` line (see Logging, [Persona destination lines](#persona-destination-lines-bav2-sr-103-as-amended-by-bdeo-sri-906)). The next retry is due after the persona's SR-3.2 wait (`createPersonaRetrySchedule`: 5 s doubling to 300 s, no cap, never shorter than a `retryAfter` the error carries). While the retry is not due, or while one retry is in flight, the persona is held and nothing is attempted for it. A failed retry advances the schedule and logs nothing (except at a newly named destination, below). The first successful attempt for the persona, prompt or notice, ends the episode with one cleared line and resets the schedule; a later failure opens a new episode and logs again. A failure from an attempt that started before the last episode change (an episode opened or cleared since; for example concurrent posts all waiting on one DM open, or a slow post that fails after a retry cleared the episode) is stale: it logs no line, opens no episode and does not advance the schedule, and its notice is re-queued in submission order (attempted again at once when no episode is open, so a genuine failure then opens one). A success from an attempt that started before the open episode opened does not end it.

**Destination changed during an episode.** An in-place change to either destination setting (`permission_prompts`, `invited.permission_prompts`), or a confirmed switch change of the channel mode, can move the destination while an episode is open. The episode keys the destinations it named by setting and value together (`NamedDestination`; b.deo SRI-702, SRI-906), so after a switch change the same value under the other setting counts as not named yet. A current (not stale) failure at a destination no line of the episode has named yet logs one more opening line naming it, with that failure's step and code, and becomes the episode's latest named cause. It never logs again for that destination in the episode, so a failure back at an earlier one logs nothing. The episode and its backoff carry on unreset. The cleared line names the destination the successful post went to, with the latest named cause.

**Attempts always finish.** An attempt that never settles would leave the persona in flight with no timer. `begin()`'s `post()` settles the attempt in a `finally`, even when the resolver throws; the poller builds a prompt's text and blocks before `begin()` and wraps everything after it in `try`/`finally` `release()`, so a throw before the post frees the persona.

**Prompts and the stuck-prompt warning** are never queued in the hold. The poller asks `begin(key)` before each attempt and makes none while the persona is held; the prompt stays untracked (no live entry) until an attempt posts it, and the next due tick derives it again (Per-tick flow step 4, **Held persona**). A request that stops being pending meanwhile is not derived again and is never posted. Closing updates and click updates are not gated: an update is not a post.

**Notices** go through `deliver`. A persona that is not held, has no notices waiting and no retry of held notices running gets the notice posted at once, in raised order. Otherwise the notice joins the persona's FIFO behind earlier ones. A failed first attempt of a notice also joins it. When the retry is due, the persona's timer attempts the held notices in order, one at a time: the first failure stops and reschedules, and after the first success the rest follow. A prompt that posts ends the episode too, and the held notices are then attempted at once. The FIFO holds at most `MAX_HELD_NOTICES_PER_PERSONA` (20): past it the oldest held notice (never the one being attempted) is dropped, logged and never posted. Each attempt re-reads the persona, its client and its destination, so a changed destination or contact is honoured, a confirmed switch change included: no held notice carries a destination, and one held across the change posts at the destination of the mode turned on (b.deo SRI-703). A retry that finds no client (the persona is not up) waits again with no line; one whose persona or client lookup throws waits the same backoff, with one line per run of throws; a persona no longer applied has its held notices dropped with one line. The timer exists only while notices are held and waiting. `cancel(key)` (a persona teardown) and `cancelAll()` (shutdown) drop held notices without posting them, with one line per persona that had notices held.

Lost-message notices (Data Flow, Inbound step 7) are notices like any other: raised through the notifier under the persona's identity, held while the persona has no validated client, sent to a channel or a `dm` destination (the DM opened when attempted) and held and retried here while the destination refuses. Inbound delivery doesn't special-case them either, and in declarative mode the loader doesn't warn about the configuration below: a posted notice reaches any persona with `delivery: all` in the destination channel. So, in declarative mode, two personas that each receive every message in the other's destination channel, with neither persona's instance able to take messages, lose each other's notices and keep raising notices about each other until either instance takes messages again. This is by design; the README (Permission prompts) and the `debug-slack-channel-bots` skill tell operators to give each persona a destination no other persona receives every message in. In fungible mode stored choices cannot set up that exchange: the loop guard holds a persona's fungible destination channel at `mentions` for every other persona, whatever is stored (`channelDeliveryFor`, b.deo SRI-305; Inbound step 4; README [Channel delivery in fungible mode](../README.md#channel-delivery-in-fungible-mode)).

**Two holds for notices.** The notifier's pre-validation queue (`persona-notifier.ts`) holds a notice while the persona has no validated client; the destination hold holds it while the destination refuses. They are separate queues, each capped at 20, and a notice can pass through both: flushed from the first when the persona comes up, then held by the second if the post fails. A persona teardown empties both, the notifier's with `forget(key)` and the hold's with `cancel(key)`, and forgets the persona's cached DM conversation (`personaDestinations.forget(key)`); nothing held is posted. `forget` drops only notices queued before the teardown's notice window opened, with its one line: a notice raised while the window is open is written to the server log and a `persona-teardown-notice` entry, never queued in either hold, so `forget` drops none of those, and `flush` posts nothing for a key whose window is open (b.jg5 SRJ-1003; [Persona teardown](#persona-teardown-bav2-sr-65-as-amended-by-bdeo-sri-307), "The notice window").

**Dry run** makes no Slack call, so nothing is ever held: the notifier logs its dry-run line before reaching the hold, and `clientFor` answers nothing in dry run, so the poller never asks the hold.

**Trail.** No trail event or field is added. Every real attempt still emits its `cscb.chat_post.attempted` or `cscb.poller.wedge_detected` event (with `error` from `safeFailureCode`); a held, skipped attempt emits nothing.

**Production caveat.** The long-lived Web API client (`persona-slack-clients.ts`) keeps the library's own retries (about 30 minutes) and rate-limit waits. So a network failure reaches the hold only after those retries are spent, and a rate-limited call is absorbed by the library; platform errors such as `missing_scope`, `not_in_channel` and `channel_not_found` reach it at once.

#### Action ID encoding (SR-3)

Block Kit buttons emit `action_id` strings of the shape `perm_(allow|deny)_<claude_instance_id>_<request_token>`, where `<request_token>` is a UUIDv4. The anchored decoder regex uses the UUIDv4 character class (`[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}`) as an outer-structure anchor — it disambiguates the rightmost boundary of the middle (underscore-bearing) `claude_instance_id` capture so embedded underscores in `cscb_<key>` remain safe. `<key>` is the persona key. CSCB does NOT validate the token's bytes; the regex shape only fixes the parse boundary (SR-1.3 + SR-3.1). The `request_id` field is no longer part of the action_id payload and is retained on `LivePermission` for logging only (SR-1.4).

#### Version pin (SR-6)

The startup gate (`runStartupGate` in `src/agent-director-startup.ts`) applies two version checks to the system-installed AD binary, in this order:

1. **The client's minimum.** AD's library-side `Client.create()` reads `dist/version-floor.json` (`.min_binary_version`), probes the binary found by `resolveSystemBinary()` and rejects one below that minimum with `ErrSystemInstallTooOld`, which the gate `instanceof`-matches → `ad-system-install-too-old`, refusal kind `client-too-old`.
2. **CSCB's Phase 1 floor (b.jg5 SRJ-203).** The gate checks the built client's `binaryVersion` against `PHASE1_FLOOR_VERSION` with `meetsPhase1Floor` (`src/ad-version-gate.ts`) → `ad-below-phase1-floor`, refusal kind `below-phase1-floor`. The floor sits above the client's minimum and refuses the client's `0.0.0-dev` sentinel and any version that does not parse. A version the client itself refuses as unparseable (`ad-system-install-unreachable`, reason `unparseable-version`) fails at Construct and never reaches the floor.

While the server runs, the runtime version re-check (`src/ad-version-gate.ts`, b.jg5 SRJ-204) applies the same two checks every 120 s (`AD_VERSION_RECHECK_INTERVAL_MS`): it calls `resolveSystemBinary()`, whose `ErrSystemInstallTooOld` is the client's minimum, then checks the reported version with `meetsPhase1Floor`. A binary that fails either stops the server with the runtime form of the same class's message; see [Graceful Shutdown](#graceful-shutdown-sr-11-event-11). A re-check that cannot run (the binary missing, unreadable, unreachable or not answering within 30 s) leaves the server running and logs one line per run of failures (b.jg5 SRJ-206; see [Runtime version re-check lines](#runtime-version-re-check-lines-bjg5-srj-205-srj-206)).

CSCB's `package.json` exact pin on `agent-director` (`0.11.0`) only governs npm resolution of AD's TypeScript shim; it does NOT participate in either check. The startup gate is the compatibility boundary — no runtime code path degrades to the prior singular-projection or coalesced-prompt behavior on version mismatch (SR-6.2). The typed-error class labels are `ad-system-install-not-found`, `ad-system-install-too-old`, and `ad-system-install-unreachable`, plus CSCB's own `ad-below-phase1-floor`; see [Startup errors](../README.md#startup-errors). See [Server-Managed Startup](#server-managed-startup-sr-11-event-1) step 1 for the gate order.

**Where the client is built and the host binary resolved (b.jg5 SRJ-121).** `Client.create()` runs only in the startup gate (`src/agent-director-startup.ts`'s production `createClient`), which the server's start (`runAgentDirectorStartupGate`) and the CLI's `initClient` (`runStartupGate`) run. `resolveSystemBinary()` is used as a value only by the runtime re-check's wiring (`src/server.ts` passes it to `installAdVersionRecheck`), the install check (`src/install-check.ts`, as `runInstallCheck`'s default resolver) and `/publish`'s check (`scripts/ad-version-check.ts`, whose `main()` passes it). Each is injected in tests (`StartupGateDeps.createClient`, the re-check's and the checks' resolver parameters), so host `bun test` never reaches the real binary; `tests/host-safety.test.ts` audits the call sites.

Operators have an alternate diagnostic entry point via `bun run install-check` (`scripts/install-check.ts`), which calls `runInstallCheck()` from `src/install-check.ts`. Its outcomes are described under `install-check.ts` and `ad-version-gate.ts` in the Module Map. The script exports `renderSuccess` (the OK block, then the Phase 1 note line when the result carries a note), `renderFailure` (the class label, the message and any detail), `main()` (called only when the script is the entry point; it appends the install-skill block to every failure but `ad-version-floor-unreadable`) and `INSTALL_CHECK_NOTE_LABEL` (`note:`), the label the note line begins with after its indent. The install-cscb skill runs the script and relays the note found under that label as printed (b.jg5 SRJ-1110).

#### API surface probe (SR-6.1)

A passing `Client.create()` proves only that the system-installed `agent-director` binary meets AD's declared `min_binary_version`. It does NOT prove the npm package's TS shim matches that binary: a shim whose `Client` lacks `getPermission`, whose `buildDecide()` omits `--request-token`, or whose catalogue lacks a required class fails silently at runtime (clicks resolve against the wrong row; error-envelope classification misses, because the client's `throwFromEnvelope` turns an err_name it has no class for into `ErrUnknownErrorName`), so the gate runs three short-circuit probes after `Client.create()` resolves and the Phase 1 floor check passes, and before the same-user stat. The probes are dependency-injected via `StartupGateDeps` so tests can drive each failure path directly; the production defaults live alongside in `src/agent-director-startup.ts`.

| Probe | Default check | Failure `classLabel` |
|---|---|---|
| `probeGetPermission` | `typeof client.getPermission === 'function'` | `ad-shim-missing-get-permission` |
| `probeErrorCatalog` | Reads the resolved `agent-director` dist file and hands its text to the exported pure `checkErrorCatalog(distText)`, which confirms a class declaration (`class <Name>` followed by whitespace) for each name in `REQUIRED_ERR_NAMES`: `ErrInvalidFlags`, `ErrPermissionRequestNotFound`, `ErrAmbiguousRequest`, `ErrTmuxKillFailed`, `ErrTmuxUnresponsive`, `ErrTmuxSessionConflict`. A name that appears only in the shim's error metadata array, with no class declaration, counts as missing. Same static-file approach as `probeDecideArgv` (the class declaration is what the client needs to build the typed error; a bare-name match would also hit the metadata array). A dist read failure reports every required name missing, with the read error in the first slot | `ad-shim-catalog-incomplete` |
| `probeDecideArgv` | `import.meta.resolve('agent-director')` → `readFileSync` of the dist entry → string-contains `--request-token` (no subprocess, no state-DB write) | `ad-shim-decide-drops-token` |

The error-catalogue check reads names in the dist text and imports none of them. The three Phase-1-only names are required because the code recognises those errors by the client's own classes, which `agent-director-errors.ts` re-exports (see the module map), and a client without their classes turns a Phase 1 binary's errors into `ErrUnknownErrorName`. A client whose dist lacks any of the six declarations fails the gate as `ad-shim-catalog-incomplete` with a non-zero exit, and the message lists the missing names. The catalogue check's unit tests pass dist text to `checkErrorCatalog` and never read the installed client's dist or call the production probe.

On any probe failure, the gate closes the Client, records the operator-readable message to `startup-errors.log`, and exits non-zero — the same shape as the SR-6 version-pin failure. The remedy in every case is the same, `CLIENT_PACKAGE_REMEDY` (`src/install-check.ts`, shared with the `ad-version-floor-unreadable` texts): check the agent-director npm package installed with CSCB, and the README's switch-over runbook section. It names no command and advises nothing else. The `ad-shim-catalog-incomplete` message says that envelopes with the missing names would arrive as `ErrUnknownErrorName` and be misclassified.

#### What this replaces

Three pre-Epic-4 mechanisms have been retired:

- The four-case per-spawn reconciliation matrix (and its sibling-stomping `updateNoLongerActive()` helper that edited a prior row's Slack message in response to another row's arrival) is gone. Sibling rows are now first-class state from the moment they appear in the plural projection.
- The click handler's prior get-then-stale-rerender branch (a refetch + "already decided" `chat.update` issued without calling decide) is gone. `decideWithToken` is the click's only AD interaction.
- The single-prompt coalescing of multiple concurrent `tool_use` blocks is gone. N parallel tool_uses → N Slack prompts.

AskUserQuestion is denied at the agent-director template (SR-3.1's `deny: ['AskUserQuestion']`) — the tool is unavailable to every CSCB-spawned bot and the prior `/ask` HTTP route + hook script have been removed.

The template also carries a narrow `allow` list (b.fae) pre-authorizing bot reads of their own persistent-memory directories. The rules are **derived per config** by `deriveMemoryReadAllowRules(personaConfig, home?)` rather than hardcoded. Each applied persona contributes its effective `claude_config_dir` (its own, else the top-level one, already resolved on the persona) — the directory `session-manager.ts` `buildSpawnParams` exports as `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` at spawn. A persona with none uses Claude Code's default `<home>/.claude` (`resolveClaudeConfigDir`, home read at call time), and a config with no personas still gets the default-dir rule. The set comes from `effectiveClaudeConfigDirs` (`persona-identity.ts`), the rule the reload plan's `configDirsChanged` shares: the distinct dirs are de-duplicated and sorted, and one rule is emitted per dir:

```
Read(//<abs-config-dir>/projects/*/memory/**)
```

So a deployment whose personas use `~/.claude-infhub` and `~/.claude` yields those two rules, but a single-config or default-only deployment yields just one. The boot install writes the rules for the applied personas, and a confirmed change that alters the set of effective config dirs rewrites them for the confirmed personas (apply step 5, [Template refresh](#template-refresh-bav2-sr-86-step-5-as-amended-by-bdeo-sri-805)); a failed refresh leaves the previous rules until the set changes again or the next start. Memory-note reads always require confirmation in Claude Code; without this rule they round-trip to a human as a native TUI permission prompt (the prompt class that wedged the relay in b.fae). **The scope is deliberately limited to `projects/*/memory/**` and must not be widened to the config-dir root** — that root holds live credentials (`settings.json` `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `.claude.json` OAuth/token content), so a root-level allow would silently pre-authorize reads of billing credentials. The `//` prefix is Claude Code's absolute-path-from-filesystem-root anchor for Read rules.

### Scheduled Prompts (cscb_cron)

The server fires scheduled prompts from a crontable into personas once per minute. The flow crosses four modules — crontable → scheduler tick → dispatcher → the server's own `/interject` → cron log — and is driven entirely by `src/cron-scheduler.ts`'s single minute-aligned timer (decision 8; no per-job timers exist).

Managed sessions learn the crontable path via the `CSCB_CRONTABLE_PATH` export documented in the [Environment Variables](#environment-variables) section.

#### Location and the start's move (bug b.avm)

Bots edit the crontable often (they self-schedule by appending), and Claude Code asks the user before every write under `.claude`, so the default sits outside `~/.claude`. With `cron_table_path` absent and `SLACK_STATE_DIR` unset it is `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cscb/crontab` (`~/.config/cscb/crontab`); with `SLACK_STATE_DIR` set it stays `<config dir>/crontab`, since that variable already moves the state out of `~/.claude` and isolates an install (a second server, a test or CI run) whose schedules must not share the per-user default. An explicit `cron_table_path`, even one naming the default's own file, is used as written and never prepared: the loader's `cron_table_path_defaulted` is true only when the key is absent or `null`. `config.ts`'s `resolveDefaultCronTablePath` is the one definition; the cron log does not move (`<config dir>/cron.log`).

Before bug b.avm, a default install's crontable was `<config dir>/crontab` (`~/.claude/channels/slack/crontab`), and bots spawned then carry that path in `CSCB_CRONTABLE_PATH` (a resume restores the row's stored environment). So once per start, before anything takes the path (Server-Managed Startup step 2a-ter), `prepareDefaultCronTable` (`cron-table-migration.ts`) creates the default's directory when the loader filled the default in, and moves a crontable left at the old path to the new one. It leaves a symbolic link at the old path, so an append through the old path, by a session still carrying it, reaches the file the scheduler reads. It never overwrites the new path (both present: one WARN, the new one used, the old one untouched) and never rewrites a line.

A step that fails before the file is at the new path changes nothing, and that start runs on the old path (`cronTablePathForStart`, written into the start-time configuration, not the reload controller's, so detection sees no change): the scheduler and every launch, the start bring-up's included (`configInEffect`), name the file whose schedules are still there, the bootstrap never creates an empty crontable at the new path, and the next start tries again. Relative prompt paths, which resolve against the crontable's own directory as given, are carried by moving `<old dir>/prompts` beside the new crontable with a link at its old name (across file systems, a link at the new name instead), and by one WARN per line that would stop resolving. The module map entry has the cases. The bootstrap's no-mkdir rule (D-Q1) still holds for every path but the default's directory, which only this preparation makes, and only for a default the loader filled in.

#### Wiring and startup

The scheduler is constructed and started in `main()` (`server.ts`) **after** `Bun.serve()` is listening, because it is its own `/interject` client — it must POST to a live listener. This is the opposite placement from `startPermissionPoller`, which starts before `Bun.serve`. It is wired on every start, dry run included: a start always has an applied configuration (the last-applied record or `config.json`), so there is no path that runs without it. One cron log is built from the config-resolved `cron_log_path` with the applied `cron_log_max_bytes` as its cap (`undefined` when the key is absent: append-only) and shared by the dispatcher and the scheduler. The dispatcher is handed the server's ACTUAL bound port (`httpServer.port`, covering port-`0` configs), that cron log, the config-resolved `cron_table_path` (the crontable the start runs on, which Server-Managed Startup step 2a-ter may have set back to the old path), and a `resolveTarget` over the applied persona config (`resolvePersonaTarget(personaConfig, target)?.key`). Any construction or `start()` failure is non-fatal — the server keeps serving without a scheduler; `shutdown()` calls `cronScheduler.stop()` alongside `stopHealthCheck`/`stopPermissionPoller`.

`start()` runs, in order: (1) the crontable bootstrap — `ensureCrontableExists`, which this `start()` is the SOLE caller of; a missing crontable is created with the template header and an info line, and the scheduler proceeds with zero schedules (a create that fails, such as under a missing directory, logs `[slack] cron-scheduler: failed to create crontable at <path>: <cause>`, and the tick's vanish path retries the create); (2) the initial read + parse of the table through the same shared load path the tick's reload step uses, each parse error becoming one `parse-error` outcome line (identity/target `-`) and each loaded line with no persona list one undeliverable `warn` line (see [Undeliverable lines](#undeliverable-lines-bn4n) below); (3) exactly one `scheduler started, N schedules loaded, M undeliverable (no persona list)` info line — the PD-4 outage-window marker, since there is no catch-up, this line is the only bound on a missed-fire window; `M` is always written, 0 included; (4) arming the tick. `start()` is failure-isolated and never throws out to the server.

#### The tick (reload → match → dispatch)

The timer is a self-re-arming `setTimeout` chain aligned to the top of each minute (not `setInterval`), so ticks are serialized — a pass never overlaps the next, which is the property the hot-reload depends on: the in-memory table is swapped between whole passes, never mid-pass. Each pass, in decision-8 loop order: (1) re-load the crontable if it changed (see [Hot-reload](#hot-reload) below) — this step never dispatches and never re-arms the timer; (2) stamp the current wall-clock minute and skip the whole pass unless it is strictly after the last-ticked minute — the **monotonic guard**, so a backwards clock jump cannot re-fire already-fired minutes (matches Vixie cron), and, because it sits *after* the reload, also the protection against a double-fire across a reload — a minute already processed is never processed again, whichever generation of the table is in memory; (3) match every in-memory schedule against that minute in **server-local time** via croner (DST is croner's, D-Q3); (4) per match, consult the at-most-once `Map<schedule instance, epoch minute>` — keyed on the compiled-schedule instance (identity), NOT raw line text, so two identical operator lines are two distinct schedules that EACH fire (plain cron semantics, PD-6); only the SAME loaded schedule reappearing twice in one pass is skipped and logged as a loud `SCHEDULER BUG` info line, otherwise the instance is recorded and the match collected; (5) prune map entries older than the current minute. All matches for the minute are handed, in crontable line order, to the dispatcher.

**No catch-up (PD-4):** a tick fires only the minute observed at its start; if a pass overruns the next minute top, that minute is simply skipped — specified behavior, not a bug. A minute with no matches does nothing and logs nothing. The `(schedule instance, minute)` at-most-once assertion is a **logged bug signal**, not the dispatch mechanism — the minute-aligned single pass already makes a double-fire structurally impossible; because the key is the compiled-schedule instance rather than raw line text, two identical operator lines are distinct schedules that each fire (PD-6) and never trip the assertion — only the same loaded schedule firing twice in one pass does. The `SCHEDULER BUG` line is an info line kind, deliberately NOT an outcome class, so it never pollutes the `grep http-error` network-failure triage view. It is likewise not the cross-reload double-fire protection — that is the monotonic guard's job. There is NO rate cap, backlog cap, busy-detection, session-state check, or queue-depth throttle anywhere in the tick (owner gate answers 1-2).

#### Hot-reload

The crontable **file**, not the in-memory copy, is the runtime source of truth. Step (1) of each tick stats the crontable and compares `(mtimeMs, size)` for *inequality* against the last successful load — not ordering, so a backwards `touch` still reloads. Unchanged means no read, no log, no work. Changed means re-read, re-parse, re-compile, and swap the array; the swap only ever replaces the whole table, and it never dispatches and never touches the timer chain. The stat follows symbolic links, so after the start's move a line appended through the old path's link changes the new file's `(mtimeMs, size)` and is picked up like any other edit.

There is deliberately **no `fs.watch`, no watcher, and no dirty flag.** A swap can only take effect at a tick anyway, and a single-file watch drops the atomic-save rename that is the mandated write pattern, so a per-tick stat is both sufficient and cheaper to reason about. A successful tick reload writes one `crontable reloaded, N schedules, M undeliverable (no persona list)` info line; `start()`'s initial load deliberately emits no such line (it has its own `scheduler started` marker).

Parse errors and undeliverable warnings are logged **once per reload, not once per tick**, because the recorded stat is updated on every successful read — including a read whose content has bad lines — so an unchanged broken file stays quiet. A mid-write read needs no special handling: the parser is PD-6-tolerant, so healthy lines survive and keep firing, and the completed write is a further stat change the next tick picks up.

**Deleted file (D-Q1).** ENOENT drops to **zero schedules immediately** — nothing stale ever fires behind a deleted crontable — forgets the recorded stat, and emits a latched `crontable vanished … — 0 schedules until it is restored` warn-kind line. The warn kind is what distinguishes this from the first-install info line. The *next* pass attempts the re-create through `cron-bootstrap.ts`: an exclusive create, so if a human or a bot restored the file with content first, the bootstrap reports `already-exists` and that content loads intact; otherwise the empty template header is created (zero schedules) and logged with re-creation wording distinct from the first-install line. A persistent re-create failure stays silent — the vanish warn already latched the condition, and it must not repeat once a minute.

**Other stat/read failures.** Any non-ENOENT errno (EACCES, EIO, …) **keeps the currently loaded schedules firing** and emits one latched warn naming the cause and the schedule count. Because a failed load never updates the recorded stat, recovery (a `chmod`, say) is picked up by the next tick's inequality check, which clears the latch and logs the normal reload line.

#### Undeliverable lines (b.n4n)

A line with no persona list (the all-bots marker) parses, loads and matches, but all-bots fan-out is not built, so it can never be delivered. The shared load path (`loadAndSwap`, which every start and reload runs) writes one `warn` line per such schedule: identity = the schedule identity, target `-`, detail `line=<n> prompt=<path> undeliverable: …` (`noPersonaListWarning`). It returns the undeliverable count that both load lines carry (`schedulerStartedLine`, `crontableReloadedLine`). No server-log line is written.

The warning carries the whole message on its own: the line names no personas, will never be delivered, how to fix it, and the README section "Crontable format" as the format reference. It does not lean on the file's header, because the server never rewrites an existing crontable (`cron-bootstrap.ts`'s D-Q1 invariant), so a crontable created by an older version keeps a header that presents the all-bots form as delivered. `tests/cron-bootstrap.test.ts` checks that the named section is a heading inside the README's Scheduled Prompts section, so renaming it fails a test.

The warning changes no dispatch: the schedule is still handed to the dispatcher each minute it matches, and the dispatcher's fire-time `fanout-deferred` record is unchanged.

#### The fire path (dispatcher → /interject → cron log)

For each match the dispatcher (`src/cron-dispatch.ts`) resolves the prompt path and reads the prompt FRESH at fire time (never cached — an edited prompt takes effect next fire), resolves the written targets to persona keys and deduplicates them, applies the D-Q5 pre-checks (skip, never truncate), and POSTs `{persona, message, sender}` (`persona` = the resolved key, or the target as written when it names no persona) to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/interject`. `sender` is the schedule identity `cscb-cron:<prompt-file-basename-without-extension>` (D-Q4) — without it `/interject` defaults `senderLabel` to `interject` and a cron fire is indistinguishable from peer-bot traffic. HTTP status maps to outcome class: 200 → `delivered`, 503 → `no-session` (decision 1 — NO retry, no queue, no `scheduleRestart`; this includes a persona that is not up, which `/interject` answers 503 even while its instance runs, b.av2 SR-6.4), 404 → `unknown-persona`, any other status or a network failure → `http-error`. Every outcome plus one per-fire summary (`delivered`/`failed` counts) is appended to the cron log. A line with no persona list (all-bots) is matched but logged `fanout-deferred` and NOT dispatched — no read, no POST — with a `delivered=0 failed=0` summary; fan-out is not yet enabled. Each load has already warned about such a line (see [Undeliverable lines](#undeliverable-lines-bn4n)).

**Same-minute matches deliver independently.** Each matched schedule is delivered on its own — its own freshly-read prompt, its own `/interject` POST with `sender` = its schedule identity, and its own outcome line and per-fire summary. When several crontable lines match the same minute for the same persona, each one arrives as its own message; they are not combined.

The cron-log outcome classes are defined once in [cron.log](#cronlog-cron_log_path) — the taxonomy there is authoritative; this subsection does not restate the class names.

**Bind constraint.** The scheduler POSTs to `127.0.0.1`, so a `bind` on a single non-loopback interface leaves no loopback listener and every fire fails connection-refused → `http-error`. `bind` must include loopback (the default `127.0.0.1`, or `0.0.0.0`) for scheduled fires to work. This is log-visible and accepted; no loopback detection is added.

## Session Lifecycle

### Connection

1. Claude Code sends POST to `/mcp` (no session ID) → `initPendingSession()` creates a pending session
2. MCP handshake completes → `server.oninitialized` fires → `handleInitialized()` waits for the session's SSE stream, then calls `roots/list`. An SSE stream that never opens, a failed `roots/list` and an empty roots list each disconnect the pending session through `closePendingSession` (`registry.ts`): the pending entry is removed, its SSE keep-alive stopped and its transport closed.
3. The first root's directory (tilde-expanded, made absolute) is matched by real path against the applied personas' working directories, and admitted only while that persona is up (`decideSessionAdmission` in `registry.ts`, over `matchPersonaByRootsPath` and the server's shared up predicate; b.av2 SR-6.3, SR-6.4). On a match to exactly one persona that is up, the pending session is promoted in place to the registered session for that persona key, with the real path as its `cwd`; a newer session for the same persona replaces the older one (logged as `Session replaced existing connection for persona …`). Registration ends the persona's not-connected episode (`forgetNotConnectedEpisode`, b.f2b), so a later disconnection is reported again. With no matching persona or an ambiguous match, the pending session is disconnected through `closePendingSession`, as in step 2.
   - **A held directory (b.av2 SR-6.3 as amended by b.jg5 SRJ-1505; SRJ-809, SRJ-810).** First, before any persona is matched, `decideSessionAdmission` asks its held-directory query (`SessionAdmissionOptions.heldDirectory`; `handleInitialized` passes the session manager's `oldLifeHeldDirectory`, which reads the one old-life hold set at call time and answers nothing before `main()` has installed it) with the roots real path (`resolveRealPath`, so a symlink resolves and a missing directory compares lexically). A directory held for an old life that may still be running answers `held` (`{ kind: 'held', directory, instanceIds }`), whichever persona names it, up or not, two personas sharing it included: the session is registered as no persona's and disconnected like an unmatched one, with no second line. A query that throws counts as held (fail safe), at the real path with no id. One line names the held directory and every held old instance id, in the hold set's begin order (`sessionHeldRefusalLine`): `[slack] Session refused: its working directory "<D>" is held for an old life that may still be running (instanceId="<id>"[, instanceId="<id>" …]) — registered as no persona's session until the hold ends (b.jg5 SRJ-810, SRJ-1505)`, or, for a query that threw, `(the held-directory query failed: <thrown> — taken as held)` in place of the ids. An answer naming no id is not held. Once the hold ends, a session from the directory is decided as below ([The old-life hold](#the-old-life-hold-bjg5-srj-809), **What a hold refuses**).
   - **Persona not up (b.av2 SR-6.4).** When the matched persona is `broken` or `retrying`, or its Slack connection is not serving, the session is refused the same way (`closePendingSession`: removed from the pending map, its keep-alive stopped and its transport closed); it is never promoted or mapped, and a session already registered for that persona is left as it is. The instance sees its MCP connection close; nothing is done to the instance or its agent-director row. One line is logged per refused attempt, so each new connection attempt the instance makes while the persona is down logs again (the line is not rate-limited), with no token and no diagnostic class label: `[slack] Session refused: persona "<name>" (key=<key>) is not up (<reason>) — not registered; its instance is kept and may register once the persona is up`, where `<reason>` is `describePersonaNotUp`'s `<outcome>: <first cause>`, or `its bring-up has not run` / `its Slack connection is not serving`. A missing working directory still matches its own persona through `resolveRealPath`'s lexical fallback, so its instance is refused here rather than logged as unmatched. The instance registers once the persona is up: the launch that follows its bring-up (the start pass, or the launch after a retry) goes through the collision ladder, whose `waiting` and `working` branches send `/mcp reconnect` to the running instance (the `working` branch once the row reads `waiting` or its pane shows it stale, b.f2b), and whose `ended`/`missing` branches resume the row (Server-Managed Startup step 5).
